AI infra startup Modal raises $750 mn at $15.7 bn valuation
Supriya Roy / Oct 14, 2026, 23:20 IST

Modal co-founders (L-R) Erik Bernhardsson and Akshat Bubna
BENGALURU : AI infrastructure startup Modal Labs, co-founded by Delhi-raised computer scientist and Olympiad gold medallist Akshat Bubna, has raised $750 million that values the company at $15.7 billion. The fundraise comes as the five-year-old company crossed $1 billion in annualised revenue run rate, fuelled by growing demand for infrastructure that powers AI applications. The latest valuation is more than three times the $4.6 billion Modal was valued at in May this year, when it raised $355 million in a Series C round. The company’s valuation has risen more than 14-fold since September 2025, when it was worth $1.1 billion. Accel led the latest round, with Kleiner Perkins joining as an investor. Existing backers Menlo Ventures, General Catalyst, Redpoint, Lux Capital and Bain Capital Ventures also participated, the company said on Wednesday. Modal said usage of its platform had tripled in the five months since its previous funding round, while the business had grown more than 15-fold year-on-year. Its annualised run rate, which reflects the pace of revenue extrapolated over a year rather than revenue earned in the preceding 12 months, has climbed from about $300 million in May to over $1 billion.
Founded in 2021 by Bubna and Swedish engineer Erik Bernhardsson, Modal provides computing infrastructure that allows companies to develop, run and scale AI applications without having to manage their own servers or computing hardware. Its platform now draws capacity from more than 20 cloud providers, allowing developers to access computing power as demand rises or falls. One of Modal’s fastest-growing businesses is Sandboxes, a product that allows AI agents to execute code in isolated environments. Launched in 2023, the product alone has reached a $300 million annualised run rate, the company said. Modal claims it has launched nearly three billion such environments to date and can support up to one million running simultaneously. The surge reflects growing adoption of AI coding agents, which need computing environments to execute programs, test results and carry out tasks. Modal said its infrastructure is used by companies including DoorDash, Cognition, Ramp and Runway, as well as robotics firms Physical Intelligence, Generalist AI and 1X. Modal is also expanding its products for AI model training and inference, the process of running trained models to generate outputs. Its latest launches include tools for training models across multiple machines and new capabilities for running AI applications. Bubna, who became the first Indian student to win gold at the International Olympiad in Informatics in 2014, previously told TOI that conventional cloud infrastructure was not designed for the demands of modern AI. In an interview last year, Bubna explained that Modal’s approach was to build its own software systems rather than depend on tools originally created for older computing applications. “One of the things programming competitions teach you is that most things are pretty solvable. You get used to solving harder problems,” he said at the time. The company has also expanded its workforce sharply. Modal had around 70 employees when Bubna spoke to TOI last year. It now employs more than 200 people across New York, San Francisco and Stockholm.

AI infrastructure management software startup ASI hits $3B valuation after raising $325M in funding
by Mike Wheatley
An artificial intelligence startup called ASI Inc. , which builds complex models of air traffic and energy grids, said today it has scored $325 million in a Series C funding, bringing its valuation to a cool $3 billion.
The round was led by Spark Capital and joined by participants including Citadel Securities, Craft Ventures, Meritech Capital, Energy Impact Partners and Andreessen Horowitz.
The startup, which used to be known as Air Space Intelligence, is an AI company that develops frontier models designed to model physical reality and simulate future scenarios, so that its customers can plan and orchestrate how they operate critical infrastructure in real time.
It caters to companies in the aviation , defense and energy industries. For instance, it works with the Federal Aviation Administration and airlines such as United Airlines Inc. and Delta Air Lines Inc. to simulate and predict what’s happening in air space, so they can plan their flight operations. It gives pilots and air traffic controllers a way to plan ahead, reduce delays and increase flight safety and efficiency.
In addition, ASI works with the U.S. Army, U.S. Air Force and others, providing them with AI-driven command-and-control software that’s used to manage their daily operations. It also helps companies in the energy sector, including grid operators, enabling them to simulate their grid operations and plan for surges in demand.
ASI founder and Chief Executive Phillip Buckendorf (pictured) said he believes that future economic growth will be dependent on giving the people who run the country’s most critical infrastructure the ability to predict and forecast scenarios ahead of time, so they can avoid failures. “While the broader tech ecosystem spent hundreds of billions teaching AI to manipulate words and generate text, ASI is deeply focused on AI systems that can manage and control physical assets,” he stressed. “This capital ensures ASI scales as America’s engine: the automated nervous system keeping the country running.”
While hundreds of billions have been spent teaching AI to manipulate words and generate videos, ASI builds AI systems that can manage and control critical physical infrastructure – where there is zero margin for error.
Today we announced our $325M Series C to scale America’s… pic.twitter.com/l133h8H92E
— ASI (@AirSpaceIntel) October 20, 2026
The round follows a significant customer win for ASI. In June, it signed an $875 million multiyear agreement with the FAA to manage future air traffic across the U.S. with its AI platform. Impressively, it won the 12-year contract ahead of bigger and better known rivals such as Palantir Technologies Inc. and Thales SE, which both made aggressive bids, according to Bloomberg .
In air traffic scenarios, ASI’s system combines data from flight paths, real-time air traffic, weather and controller staffing to predict congestion and devise ways to get around problems and avoid delays. The FAA implemented the software at Dulles International Airport in Washington DC last month, and plans to expand it to all major U.S. airports in future.
The contract was a significant win for ASI, making the startup one of only four technology companies to land a federal contract of that size since 2000. Since then, ASI has secured another big contract with the U.S. Army. Earlier this month, it announced it had agreed a five-year deal worth $99 million to supply the military with AI software for its command-and-control program. Another big customer is National Grid USA Service Company Inc., which uses ASI’s software for planning purposes.
Going forward, ASI said the money from today’s round will help it expand further into the aviation, defense and energy sectors and also target new industries such as logistics. It’s also planning to grow its research and engineering teams with an eye to expanding the capabilities of its software.

Physical AI startup SiMa.ai, which has deep Indian roots and a major research and development centre in Bengaluru, raised another $150 million . Emergent, River Mobility, Navi, Slice and Pixxel also secured more than $100 million each during the quarter.
Despite the decline in overall funding, early-stage deals crossed the $1 billion mark in Q3. The quarter also saw six startup listings, including NSE, Rentomojo, Molbio, Milky Mist, Leap India and Purple Style Labs. Six startups shut down operations during the quarter.

This amount included 46 growth and late-stage deals totalling $1.89 billion, along with 194 early-stage deals worth $1.01 billion. Additionally, there were 26 undisclosed deals during the period.
[Q-o-Q and M-o-M trend]
Q3 2026 saw a modest recovery in startup funding compared to the same quarter last year. Total funding rose to $2.9 billion from $2.78 billion in Q3 2025, but remained below the $4 billion recorded in Q3 2024. September emerged as a strong month for funding, as startups raised more than $1 billion for the third time in 2026. February and June were the previous two months to cross the $1 billion mark, with each recording around $2 billion in funding. The September uptick helped Q3 close above the funding level recorded in the year-ago quarter.
[Top 15 growth-stage deals]
In Q3 2026, India’s top 15 growth and late-stage deals reflected strong investor interest in mobility, AI and fintech, along with bets across consumer and deeptech sectors. Simple Energy topped the list after raising $182 million in its Series C round, followed by physical AI startup SiMa.ai, which secured $150 million in Series C funding. AI startup Emergent raised $130 million , while electric two-wheeler maker River Mobility secured $120 million. Fintech firms Navi and Slice raised $100 million each, while electric mobility platform Yulu followed with $93 million. EV maker Ultraviolette raised $85 million, while AI startups Ema and Sarvam AI secured $77 million and $74 million, respectively. Wearable tech startup Ultrahuman raised $70 million, while The Pizza Bakery secured $56 million. Healthtech startup Nua raised $50 million, followed by Third Wave Coffee at $43 million and aerospace and defence company Raghu Vamsi Aerospace Group at $40 million.
[Top 15 early-stage deals]
Early-stage activity remained strong in Q3 2026, led by Pixxel’s $100 million Series A and Airbound’s $37 million Series A. Yuma Energy followed with $35 million, while Centricity and InRisk Labs raised $30 million and $27 million, respectively. Most of the top deals fell in the $15–25 million range, reflecting steady investor interest in early-stage companies.
Spacetech, fintech, deeptech and mobility featured prominently among the top deals. Data centre startup CtrlS raised $25 million, while foodtech firm Arboreal Bioinnovations secured $24 million . Business Nextgen Finance and Runable raised $21.7 million and $21 million, respectively. NeoGeo, Nexedge Capital and QNu Labs raised $20 million each, while Gravity, Piston and Plaza rounded out the list at $15 million each.
[Mergers and acquisitions]
The Indian startup ecosystem saw 33 merger and acquisition transactions in Q3 2026, covering sectors such as fintech, healthtech, AI, edtech, spacetech and e-commerce. Some of the notable deals included Samara Capital’s $120 million acquisition of stakes in Associated Road Carriers and Calyx Container Terminal, ITC’s $65 million acquisition of Yoga Bar and Udaan’s $52 million acquisition of Swiggy’s supply chain platform Lynk. Aurum PropTech agreed to acquire Housing.com’s parent in a $46.2 million share swap deal, while Ananta Capital acquired a majority stake in Phitku for $10.6 million. PhysicsWallah also acquired a controlling stake in Sarrthi IAS for $7.5 million. Nuvacore startup raises hundreds of millions at $2.5 billion valuation for new data center processor
Nuvacore, a six-month-old startup, is raising significant funds for its central processor development aimed at data centers. The company plans to optimize chip design for common data center and AI computations, avoiding traditional architecture limitations. Founded by former Apple executive Gerard Williams, Nuvacore has already secured previous funding led by Sequoia Capital. Investor interest in semiconductor startups has increased significantly in recent months, surpassing previous funding totals.

Six-month-old microchip startup Nuvacore , which does not yet have a product, is raising hundreds of millions of dollars at a roughly $2.5 billion valuation to develop a new central processor designed for data centers , according to two people familiar with the fundraising.
Nuvacore is seeking to raise the funds as the appetite for central processors has swollen due to the thirst for data-crunching capacity to power chatbots such as Anthropic's Claude. CPUs perform vital functions as traffic controllers for Nvidia's AI chips and run autonomous AI software known as agents.
The roughly $2.5 billion valuation has not been previously reported. The Information reported previously that Nuvacore was raising $200 million or more. The funding round has not closed, and the people cautioned that the valuation and size of the capital raise could change.
Advt
Intel and Advanced Micro Devices, which use x86 technology, have long dominated the data center CPU market. Companies designing chips based on Arm's technology - found inside Amazon and Microsoft custom CPUs - have also attempted to make inroads in the data center market.
Nuvacore has not yet developed a product. Last month, it described an unconventional design strategy: to build the core functionality of the chip before committing to an architecture such as the x86 used by Intel and AMD, or Arm, which is used in most mobile phones.
The design strategy will allow the company's engineers to avoid the limitations and requirements of specific architectures and optimize a design for the type of computations that are most common in data centers and AI infrastructure, Nuvacore said.
Nuvacore declined to comment.
The San Jose, California-based startup was founded by renowned engineers Gerard Williams, John Bruno and Ram Srinivasan. Williams, a former Apple executive, sold a prior startup called Nuvia to Qualcomm for $1.4 billion in 2021.
Nuvacore earlier this year announced a seed funding round led by Sequoia Capital. It joins a series of young chip startups that have sought billion-dollar valuations before releasing a product as investor appetite for AI hardware companies has returned.
Over the past decade, Silicon Valley venture capital firms have taken much less interest in hardware than software because of hardware's longer development cycles, higher capital needs and the industry's cyclical demand.
Advt
Investors put about $10.7 billion into semiconductor startups in the first five months of 2026, already outpacing the $12.2 billion raised globally in all of 2025, according to Crunchbase data.
Earlier this year, Intel said it could not manufacture enough chips to meet demand, and was able to sell products it had previously determined were too faulty for sale. AMD also described swelling CPU sales in a recent results conference call with analysts.
Shares in both companies have risen more than 180% this year.
Nvidia launched a CPU called Vera this year. CEO Jensen Huang has said the company expects to sell $20 billion worth of its Vera CPU in this fiscal year, which ends in January.

candidates.text:
Year-old startup Flapping Airplanes has wowed Silicon Valley with an impressive founding team and a mission to find ways to train large models with less data. On Wednesday, the company announced it had raised a $1 billion Series A round, co-led by Index and Lux, reportedly at a $6 billion valuation.
The round comes just nine months after the company launched with a $180 million seed round from GV, Sequoia, and Index. That seed round had valued the company at $1.5 billion, so its valuation just quadrupled.
Other participants in the new round included earlier backers Sequoia, GV, and Kleiner Perkins. Valor, Atreides, Kleiner Perkins, A*, and Nvidia are also investors in the company.
Flapping Airplanes was founded by Aidan Smith and brothers Asher and Ben Spector. Smith is a former founder and Thiel fellow who worked at the brain implant company Neuralink during college. Asher Spector was a statistics PhD at Stanford, while Ben Spector was a computer science PhD student at Stanford and founded Prod while at MIT.
Prod is an almost secret-society, five-year-old student-run startup accelerator that has “become one of the most powerful talent incubators in Silicon Valley,” wrote Sequoia partner David Cahn , a Flapping Planes investor, in a post earlier this year explaining why he invested. Together, the founders “are building the ‘young person’s AGI lab,’” as Cahn described it.
The founders describe their work as “the world’s most complete megakernel framework. It can perform entire training runs, serve inference, play video games, and even do all three simultaneously in a single kernel.” (A kernel is a program that runs on a GPU, and a megakernel bundles many tasks into one program.)
The founders claim the framework “can overlap memory-bound inference with compute-bound training,” meaning it can run a task that spends most of its time waiting for data to be fetched alongside one that spends most of its time doing math, so the chip is rarely sitting idle. The premise is that AI has barely scratched the surface of what GPUs can do, and they believe it can create intelligent systems “without ingesting half the internet.”
The goal is systems that cost less to train and run. “A model that’s a million times more data efficient is probably a million times easier to put into the economy,” Asher Spector told TechCrunch shortly after the startup launched.
They now have a fresh $1 billion to hire and attempt to turn that goal into reality.

With AI coding agents now producing a large and growing share of the world's code, the burden has changed from writing code to validating it. Every change still has to be built and tested before it can be merged, a step known as continuous integration, or CI.

CI is the most variable workload a company runs: a single customer's demand regularly jumps from zero to tens of thousands of CPUs and back again. TypeSafe AI announced on October 9, 2026 that it has raised an $870 million Series A at a $7.5 billion valuation, led by Andreessen Horowitz with participation from Sequoia Capital, existing investor DCVC, and angel investors. Andreessen Horowitz general partner Martin Casado is joining the company’s board.
Round Terms and Investors
Andreessen Horowitz confirmed it is leading the investment in a post dated October 9, 2026 and bylined by Jennifer Li, Sarah Wang, Martin Casado, Marc Andreessen, and Ben Horowitz. Li and Casado are general partners focused on the firm’s infrastructure investing, Wang is a general partner on its growth team, and Andreessen and Horowitz are the firm’s cofounders and general partners.
TypeSafe’s own announcement is a short post addressed to developers, businesses, and potential recruits; the company disclosed the dollar amount, the valuation, and Casado’s board seat in a footnote to that post.
The System One Model Behind the Round
TypeSafe released Jev in early access on September 15, 2026, after two years in stealth, and said it is bringing developers off its waitlist. In the launch post , founder Diogo Almeida described Jev as the first entry in a new model class the company calls System One, designed for rapid, structured decision-making inside software.
According to TypeSafe’s documentation , Jev takes typed questions and evaluates them against a supplied state, returning structured results without generating or parsing text. The results arrive as typed values with probability distributions, so code can branch, sort, and route on them directly. The company exposes three primitives: Choice picks one option out of a provided list; Score grades the state against a rubric; and Noul returns a 0–1 answer to whether a given statement is true. Choice and Score also return confidence values, and all three question types can be combined in one API call, where each is evaluated independently and concurrently against the same state.
Almeida wrote that TypeSafe built a new stack focused entirely on automation: a new model architecture, a parallel sampler, and a training method the company calls Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD). He said Jev achieves similar intelligence to existing large language models on System One tasks while running two orders of magnitude faster, with end-to-end response times of 70 to 500 milliseconds, a range the post states can be 40 to 200 times faster than frontier models at comparable intelligence for System One–shaped queries. Because outputs are type-safe structured values defined in advance, Almeida wrote, the model never makes type errors and cannot hallucinate.
Published pricing is $0.042 per million input tokens, with output tokens free. The company states that the 193.6-times-faster and 444.6-times-cheaper figures on its homepage come from its workflow evaluations, and it cautions that those numbers are on the higher end of real-world gains. It also notes that the evaluation workflows were built by members of its model capabilities team and that some bias could exist.
Almeida wrote that at OpenAI he helped develop instruction-following methods for language models, work he said became the research behind ChatGPT. The System One name references Daniel Kahneman’s book Thinking, Fast and Slow and its contrast between quick, intuitive System 1 thinking and slower, deliberate System 2 reasoning. Jev is named after William Stanley Jevons; the company said it expects machine intelligence to follow the path of coal, for which steam-engine efficiency gains led to increased demand.

It characterized Jev as roughly 1/100 to 1/500 the cost of frontier models while being 100 times faster for classification tasks at comparable accuracy, passing model decisions straight into code as typed values rather than text that software must then parse.
In an October 7, 2026 case study , TypeSafe reported that Jack & Jill, a talent marketplace where AI agents match candidates with hiring teams, replaced Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite for 100% of calls in a key stage of its candidate-matching pipeline within 10 days of its first test. As AI agents spread across the industry, investment is piling into an infrastructure layer that skips long, human-readable text responses and instead hands software a judgment it can consume directly. The promise of solving speed, cost and reliability at once is moving investors fast.
TypeSafe AI sits at the center of that shift. Last month the company came out of stealth with a $40 million seed round for its structured-decision model, Jev. Unlike a conversational LLM, Jev doesn’t generate sentences — it returns a “typed decision” with an attached probability, chosen from a schema the developer defines in advance. Because the output shape is fixed ahead of time, the company says it can’t produce an answer outside that schema, and because it samples in parallel rather than generating tokens one at a time, it responds far faster.
The company was founded in 2024 by Diogo Almeida, Erik Gafni and Sasha Sheng. CEO Almeida previously co-developed reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) at OpenAI and worked on InstructGPT, ChatGPT and GPT-4.
TypeSafe AI said it closed an $870 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz, with Sequoia Capital and existing investor DCVC participating. The round values the company at $7.5 billion — a jump of dozens of times its seed-round valuation in under a month. a16z general partner Martin Casado is joining the board.
Rather than spell out a spending plan, the announcement stuck to a direction: push everything people like about Jev to the extreme, ship more machine-native models, and keep building out the infrastructure for “smart software.” The company says a third of the Fortune 500 are already using Jev and that it has saved production customers millions of dollars — claims that, as with the seed announcement, come from the company itself and haven’t been independently verified.
The competitive picture hasn’t shifted much. When TypeSafe first emerged, Earendil CTO Armin Ronacher — whose company builds the open-source model harness Pi — said Jev was “alone” in its category for now, but that “once people know this works, competitors will show up.” A month later, no direct rival in the same category has clearly emerged. The closest alternatives remain inference-acceleration infrastructure that runs existing frontier models faster and cheaper on dedicated chips, and guardrail layers that score LLM outputs after the fact. The sheer size of this round suggests investors still see the category as TypeSafe’s alone to lose.

Fractile Secures £577M Series C to Scale AI Chip Production
Fractile has raised £577 million in Series C funding as the London-based chipmaker prepares to deploy its inference hardware in data centers by 2027.
Elena Whitmore
·
30 October 2026 09:45
·
2 min read
·
14,436 reads
Google'a Ekle
Fractile , the London-based artificial intelligence hardware startup, has secured £577 million in a Series C funding round. Official filings at Companies House confirm the capital injection, marking the firm's largest fundraising effort to date.
Strategic Capital Allocation
The funding was executed through nine share allotment returns filed between 15 October and 28 October. The breakdown of the equity classes includes:
Series C-1: £147.8 million
Series C-2: £37.4 million
Series C-3: £392.2 million
The allotments reflect a significant valuation surge for the company, which was in discussions earlier this year for a pre-money valuation of approximately $6.5 billion. The total raise, when converted, equates to roughly $774 million.
Hardware Ambitions
Founded in 2022 by Walter Goodwin and Yuhang Song , Fractile specializes in inference chips designed to accelerate the response times of large AI models. The company aims to reduce the time required for complex AI workloads from one month to a single day by keeping data adjacent to processing transistors.
Market demand is currently driven by a severe scarcity of high-performance compute hardware. Anthropic has already signaled its intent to integrate Fractile technology, placing an initial order valued at $250 million. The hardware is slated for deployment in 2027.
The Road to 2027
Despite the substantial capital backing, the company faces a critical test. Fractile has yet to ship a production-ready chip to customers. The firm previously utilized its Series B funds to establish engineering operations in London , Bristol , San Francisco , and Taipei . The current infusion of cash provides the runway necessary to transition from design to mass manufacturing.
Investors are betting on the firm's architecture to outperform existing solutions. Competition is fierce. Cerebras and Etched have set high benchmarks for valuation in the inference space. Success hinges on Fractile hitting its 2027 delivery targets. The market is watching. The hardware must perform.

Legal AI startup Harvey closed a $550 million growth‑stage round on Oct. 1, 2026, pushing its post‑money valuation to $15.5 billion. The capital will fund product acceleration and deeper market penetration as AI‑driven legal tech adoption spikes among law firms.
Harvey announced a $550 million financing on Oct. 1, 2026, valuing the legal‑AI platform at $15.5 billion post‑money. The round, the largest for the company to date, comes as its annual recurring revenue (ARR) sits at $400 million, implying a roughly 14× ARR multiple on the new valuation. ## Deal Terms The funding round was led by a syndicate of venture firms (details were not disclosed) and will be deployed to expand Harvey’s product suite, scale its engineering team, and accelerate go‑to‑market efforts in North America and Europe. The infusion follows a broader surge of capital into AI‑centric SaaS businesses, underscoring investor confidence in the legal‑tech vertical’s growth trajectory. ## Market Context Recent ILTA survey data show that 40 % of law firms prioritized generative AI over any other technology in the past year, with cloud SaaS applications trailing at 25 %. Within that AI landscape, Microsoft Copilot leads usage at 76 % of firms, while Harvey is adopted by 43 % of respondents, ranking just behind Copilot, Claude (44 %), and Thomson Reuters CoCounsel (44 %). Token consumption on Harvey’s platform has risen 14‑fold in the last six months, reflecting both deeper integration into legal workflows and the looming shift from subscription‑based pricing to consumption‑based models. The funding positions Harvey to double‑down on its open‑weight model strategy, compete directly with the newly launched OpenAI Astra for Law and Google Gemini Enterprise for Legal, and potentially lock in enterprise contracts before the market pivots to token‑based pricing. As law firms grapple with legacy on‑prem accounting systems—still present in 52 % of firms—the move toward cloud‑native, AI‑enhanced solutions like Harvey could accelerate the displacement of traditional software stacks, reshaping the competitive dynamics of the legal‑tech ecosystem.
Why It Matters
Harvey’s fresh war‑chest enables it to outpace rivals in product velocity, particularly against Microsoft Copilot and Anthropic’s Claude, which currently dominate law‑firm AI usage. By expanding its model‑training capabilities and bolstering its token‑pricing infrastructure, Harvey can lock in higher‑margin consumption revenue, pressuring competitors that remain tied to subscription models. For Thomson Reuters, which is investing $40 million in its own legal LLM, Harvey’s scale and market share intensify the race for data‑rich, open‑weight models, likely prompting faster feature roll‑outs and pricing adjustments across the sector.
For investors, the deal validates the premium placed on AI‑enabled SaaS platforms that address high‑touch, regulated verticals. The 14× ARR multiple signals that capital markets are willing to bet on deep‑stack AI integration as a defensible moat, setting a benchmark for future legal‑tech valuations and influencing fund allocation toward similar vertical AI plays.
Key Points
Harvey raised $550 million, lifting its valuation to $15.5 billion.
Post‑money ARR stands at $400 million, implying roughly a 14× ARR multiple.
40 % of surveyed law firms identified generative AI as their top technology focus.
Harvey is used by 43 % of firms, trailing only Microsoft Copilot, Claude, and Thomson Reuters CoCounsel.
Token usage on Harvey’s platform grew 14‑fold over six months.
Analysis
The $550 million raise places Harvey at a $15.5 billion valuation, translating to an approximate 14× ARR multiple—well above the typical 6‑9× range for high‑growth SaaS. This premium reflects the market’s appetite for AI‑first platforms that can embed deep learning models into regulated workflows, where switching costs are high and data moats are defensible. As law firms accelerate AI adoption, the shift toward token‑based consumption pricing could unlock higher gross margins for providers that master usage analytics and cost‑control. Harvey’s capital will likely fund model‑training infrastructure, expanding its open‑weight AI stack to compete with OpenAI’s Astra for Law and Google’s Gemini Enterprise for Legal. For investors, the deal underscores a broader trend: vertical AI SaaS firms are attracting mega‑rounds at multiples that reward both revenue growth and strategic data assets. The financing also raises the bar for comparable legal‑tech startups, pressuring them to demonstrate scalable token economics and robust enterprise pipelines to justify similar valuations. In a market where legacy on‑prem systems still dominate, Harvey’s cloud‑native approach could accelerate the displacement of entrenched vendors, reshaping the competitive landscape and setting a new valuation benchmark for AI‑driven legal SaaS.

Five robotics startups raise $510M as investors chase physical AI
What's the deal? Five robotics startups — ICON , Mecka AI , MMI , Multiply Labs , and Ultra — raised a combined $510 million in the week of October 12, spanning construction, surgery, data training, drug manufacturing, and warehouse automation.
The biggest round: ICON, which builds 3D-printing construction robots, raised a $200 million Series D co-led by Baillie Gifford and funds managed by BlackRock . It plans to build a new R&D center, develop new construction systems, and expand its US footprint.
ICON has worked with the Department of War since 2020 on military housing and public infrastructure. It has won more than $370 million in government contracts and built more than 270 homes.
Who else raised? MMI, which makes robotic tools for micro- and supermicro surgery, secured a $125 million Series D led by BioStar Capital Dealroom has a profile for this one. Try Dealroom → . It has deployed nearly 50 of its Symani systems worldwide, used in more than 3,500 surgeries, and will fund US expansion.
Multiply Labs raised a $75 million Series B led by NantWorks for robots that manufacture cell and gene therapies. It sells systems directly to customers, letting them own their supply chain in a heavily regulated industry.
Mecka AI, which builds hardware and sensors to collect egocentric data for training robots, raised a $60 million Series B led by Sequoia . That came four months after $60 million across two undisclosed rounds in June. The company says it is on track for $300 million in run-rate revenue by year-end, after crossing $100 million in June.
Ultra closed a $50 million Series A for two-armed warehouse robots that pack and sort orders. Unlike its peers, Ultra leases hardware monthly, with software supplied through a partnership with Physical Intelligence .
Why now? Training data is in high demand among investors, and specialised robots — for surgery, drug manufacturing, and construction — are moving from labs into regulated real-world use.
The signal: The week's deals skipped general-purpose humanoids entirely, a reminder that capital is flowing across the full robotics stack — from data pipelines to task-specific machines — not just the flashiest category.

Humanoid developer Agility now expects to raise $465M in SPAC deal
By Eugene Demaitre | October 30, 2026
Digit 5 includes redesigned legs and new batteries for commercial use. Source: Agility Robotics
Humanoid robotics developers continue to raise millions of dollars. Agility Robotics Inc. and Churchill Capital Corp XI today said that they expect Agility to raise about $465 million in its proposed merger with the special-purpose acquisition company, or SPAC.
According to Agility, the gross capital raise includes:
About $164 million from Churchill XI’s trust account
Approximately $201 million from a common stock PIPE (private investment in public equity) committed at $10 per share, led by Foxconn with participation from existing and new institutional investors
$100 million of equity funding already received following the announcement of the business combination
That total is less than the $620 million that Agility predicted at a $2.5 billion valuation when it first announced the planned business combination in June. The Robot Report has reached out to the company for comment and will add it if we get a response.
“Agility is expected to enter the public markets well capitalized to execute its planned investments in commercial expansion and support growing customer demand,” stated the Salem, Ore.-based company .
Agility expects to close the SPAC transaction, subject to shareholder approval and the customary closing conditions, on Nov. 4. The company has claimed that it will be the first U.S. publicly traded, pure-play humanoid supplier with commercial deployments.
Agility gets Digit ready for customers
Last month, Agility unveiled its Digit 5 humanoid, which had new legs (and possibly wheels ) and is designed to work safely alongside people and support a range of workflows. Last week, Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer, and Pras Velagapudi, chief technology officer at the company, spoke about humanoid advances at RoboBusiness 2026.
Agility this month also chose Nyobolt for fast recharging, which it said will enable its robots to operate for more than 20 hours a day.
The company said it is “on track to begin deliveries to early-access customers in the first half of 2027, with general availability targeted for the end of 2027.” Agility also said it has more than $300 million in committed multi-year orders for Digit 5.
Humanoid use cases are growing
Digit continues to make progress in live operations. In a September S-4 statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Agility reported $1.8 million in net sales in 2025. Its customers across nine sites include Toyota , Mercado Libre , and Schaeffler .
AGCO this month announced plans to deploy Digit in its agricultural machinery factory in Kansas.
And this week, Agility said it is expanding its partnership with GXO Logistics, implementing humanoids in North Carolina and Tennessee.
Humanoid companies continue fundraising, acquisitions
Agility’s investors include NVIDIA (with whom it also expanded its relationship), Amazon, SoftBank Vision Fund 2, Schaeffler, Foxconn, Abico, DCVC, and Playground Global. The company said that all existing shareholders will roll their equity into the combined company and will be subject to a 180-day lock-up at closing.
Some of the top funding rounds for humanoid companies so far this year include Neura Robotics ‘ $1.4 billion Series C, XPeng Robotics ‘ $900 million Series A, AI 2 Robotics ‘ $735 million Series C, and Apptronik ‘s $520 million Series A-X.
Top acquisitions include UBTECH ‘s purchase of Fenglong Electric for $249 million and Faraday Future ‘s purchase this week of FF Robotics.

Armadin Raises $255.5 Million Series B to Scale Effective Autonomous Security
News provided by
Armadin
Oct 01, 2026, 06:00 ET

Funding brings Armadin's valuation to over $2.5 billion just seven months after its launch as AI compresses the time between vulnerability discovery and exploitation
PALO ALTO, Calif. , Oct. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Armadin, an AI-native cybersecurity company building effective autonomous security, today announced it has raised $255.5 million in Series B funding co-led by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) and Accel that brings the company's valuation to over $2.5 billion. The round includes participation from new investors Bain Capital Ventures (BCV) and Redpoint. Existing investors 8VC, Ballistic Ventures, Google Ventures, In-Q-Tel, Kleiner Perkins, and Menlo Ventures also returned, reflecting their continued confidence, bringing Armadin's total funding to $445 million.
Seven months after emerging from stealth, Armadin is running agentic attack campaigns in production for Fortune 500 enterprises and government customers. As frontier AI models compress the time between vulnerability disclosure and working exploit, periodic penetration tests cannot keep pace. Scanner output fails in a different way, because it scores each finding in isolation. Armadin deploys an autonomous swarm of specialized agents that reason like a skilled adversary across the attack surface, chaining individually low-severity weaknesses into validated kill chains. Those chains run from unauthenticated remote code execution at the perimeter through lateral movement to full cloud compromise. Enterprise and government security teams see the exact attack paths an adversary would use in production today, along with the blast radius of each, and sever them before they are exploited.
"Offense is uniquely advantaged right now," said Kevin Mandia, CEO of Armadin. "AI lets an attacker find and chain weaknesses faster than any human team can respond. The only way to build a defense that keeps pace is to train it against the best offense available, every day. That is what we built. With a16z and Accel co-leading and the support of every investor in this round, we are going to put that offense to work for the enterprises and government agencies defending the world's most critical systems."
Armadin will use the investment to scale its agentic security platform, and to scale its research, training, and go-to-market efforts.
"Against agentic adversaries, the best defense is a great offense powered by AI. That was our conviction when we led Armadin's Series A, and it's even more pressing today," said Ping Li, Partner at Accel. "In less than a year, Armadin has set the standard for AI-powered offensive security and remediation across enterprises and governments, and we're excited to keep partnering with them."
"Every major platform shift creates a new generation of security leaders, and AI is the biggest shift we've seen," said David George, General Partner at Andreessen Horowitz. "Kevin has been on the front lines of the most consequential breaches in history, and he has built a team that pairs elite red teamers with world-class AI engineers. We invested because we believe Armadin will become the defining security company of the AI era."
About Armadin
Armadin is an AI-native cybersecurity company delivering the definitive offensive security platform to identify and eliminate an organization's exploitable risks. As the threat of AI-driven threats escalates, Armadin empowers enterprises to proactively secure their environments. Armadin's platform safely delivers the most comprehensive and powerful AI Hyperattacks to identify new and novel attack paths before adversaries can exploit them. Led by CEO Kevin Mandia, Armadin is a group of engineers, researchers, and hackers on a mission to create effective autonomous security.
For more information, visit www.armadin.com .

candidates.snippet: Warhound raises $200M to engineer war dogs and arm them with Anduril gear TechCrunch
candidates.text:
Colossal Biosciences’ Ben Lamm and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey had an idea to genetically engineer war dogs for the U.S. military, law enforcement, and other emergency response teams. On Thursday, that idea came out of stealth as Warhound , backed by $200 million in funding from investors including Sequoia, 8VC, Corner Ventures, and In-Q-Tel, a venture firm backed by the CIA and other U.S. intelligence agencies. The round values the company at $1.2 billion.
Warhound’s dogs, which do not exist yet, will take on tasks that are dangerous for humans or difficult for machines, such as bomb detection, searches, and other specialized operations. In its launch announcement, the company said that more than 80% of the U.S. military’s working dogs come from Europe, and less than half of them are fit for service.
That means the supply of working dogs is dwindling, and the U.S. increasingly relies on foreign nations for dogs that play an important role in the military and in law enforcement. Warhound aims to change that. The hope is that Colossal can use its technology to engineer dogs with “characteristics suited to demanding missions,” the company said in a press release.
Lamm told TechCrunch he met Luckey about a year ago at a conference, where Luckey said more should be done for the military’s working dogs. The two kept in touch, and Lamm researched how working dogs are bred. He learned that many of them do not make it through training because of inherited predispositions to problems like poor eyesight or the high possibilities of cancer, hip dysplasia, or muscle atrophy.
Lamm believed dogs could be enhanced for health, longevity, and “for things like speed and agility or enhance olfactory sensors for bomb sniffing and whatnot,” he said. His team studied top-performing working dog breeds — the Belgian Malinois and German Shepherd — taking cell lines (living cells grown in a lab) from them and putting them in a biobank. From there, the team will edit the dogs’ genes, adding ones that will improve performance and removing ones that will not, to create “a new type of dog.”
Anduril, meanwhile, will provide software and hardware, such as protection vests and goggles, to assist the dogs and their handlers with situational awareness and coordination. Lamm said to imagine, for example, bulletproof vests with data sensors that send information back to the handlers so they can better understand what is happening.
“The idea is, if we make the dog safer, make it healthier, make it perform better, it’s going to perform better in the line of duty,” Lamm said. He added that Anduril’s additions will make the dogs safer and healthier beyond their genetics, “on top of the dog, not in the dog.” He believes the enhancements will also better protect the dogs’ human handlers.
Luckey is a partner in the venture but owns no equity in it, Lamm told TechCrunch. Colossal owns equity in the business and supports it by licensing its technology.
Colossal is currently known for its de-extinction efforts to bring back animals like the dodo and the mammoth . As Lamm previously told TechCrunch, the company has been using AI, buying and building technology to help with gene cloning and with identifying and copying animal genes.
Lamm said the first batch of dogs is about to be cloned and incubated, with births expected early next year and service ideally beginning within two years. Viagen, another Colossal-owned company, will partner with Warhound to clone the dogs. Lamm said Viagen’s technology has a high cloning success rate, and Colossal already uses it in its program to protect endangered species.
Warhound doesn’t know yet how much it will charge for the dogs, but it expects to sell to first responders, the Department of Defense, military service groups, and police forces. Asked about government approval, Lamm said the company has briefed many government groups about the business.
Asked about civilian safety once genetically enhanced dogs enter service, Lamm said each dog will be trained like any military working dog and managed by whoever buys it.
The company said it is working under the guidance of the American Humane Society to help certify Warhound’s training program for the new dogs. The hope is also that when these new military dogs retire, they will enter the Society’s Military Working Dog Reunification Program, which provides homes for retired military dogs — or another program the Society offers to help dogs.
When reached for comment, the American Humane Society said, “We applaud Warhound and Colossal for inviting the country’s first national humane organization, which is grounded in science and ethics, to have a seat at the table. We look forward to working with them to help ensure the animals in their care are treated humanely.”
This piece was updated to add Corner Ventures as an investor and to add the statement from the American Humane Society.

Supabase raises another $150M to build the backend for AI coding from Singapore
New funding comes months after $500M raise and includes strategic acquisition
Jon Russell

Welcome back to Asia Tech Review, your curated digest to keep up to date with tech news across Asia.
Supabase might just be the best example of a new tech startup in Singapore. It has built a fast-growing and global business that’s been backed with over $1 billion from investors across the world. And it’s building core tools for the agentic era. Today, we look at its newest round, an acquisition and its future goals.
To keep up with our issues, follow us on LinkedIn or WhatsApp . Please do share Asia Tech Review with people you know who want to get smart about Asia tech.
For news as it happens, follow ATR Bulletin , our real-time news site that keeps you in the know.
The tech startup blueprint Singapore wants to see more of
Supabase, the Singapore-based database platform that helps developers build apps and software, closed a $150 million funding round , just four months after it announced a $500 million Series F round.
The round is led by GIC, the Singapore sovereign fund, and it includes Google’s CapitalG fund for the first time. That’s notable as one of the main competitors of Supabase’s developer stack is Google-owned Firebase. Still, Supabase CEO Paul Copplestone said the fund’s “connections to the broader Alphabet ecosystem will be invaluable as we build for our next level of growth.”
You don’t typically see a smaller round like this follow a huge raise like Supabase’s Series F, but in this case the startup’s recent growth spurt is such that it appears to need the funds to support continuing to accelerate its trajectory.
“Supabase is now adding more than 1M users and 4M databases per month with 70% of new databases created by agents or AI-driven tools. The growth follows a 600% year-over-year increase in databases reported in June, when agents were already deploying the majority of new databases on the platform,” the company wrote.
Supabase has raised over $1 billion in total from investors that include Accel, Peak XV, Craft, Coatue, Y Combinator, Stripe, Salesforce Ventures and Figma.
It’s worth recalling what Supabase does. It provides a set of backend tools to enable developers to quickly build and develop apps, websites and other software using a central resource to manage files, authentication, databases and more. In the agentic era which allows software to be created in minutes or hours not days, that’s a particularly key tech stack as Supabase’s numbers seem to show.
That explains why, alongside the funding round, it announced that it acquired a startup called Turso , which allows databases to be provisioned on demand. That makes perfect sense for Supabase since vibe- and agentic-coding is sending its numbers skyrocketing, it needs the tools to support faster creation of databases and the plumbing beyond apps, websites and more.
Whether you create a web app for friends, a private CRM tool for your company or a new product for an existing customer base, Supabase wants to make its tools the go to for Claude, ChatGPT or bots like Muse, Grok Bot or Dots.
Singapore’s sovereign wealth funds are doubling down on AI startup investments
Jon Russell
·
Jul 10
Read full story
Supabase is the closest example to a modern Singapore tech success story. Its founders aren’t Singaporean, but they met in the country during a cohort for Entrepreneur First.
They didn’t start their business in EF, the accelerator programme that left Singapore in 2023 , but they’ve grown a multi-billion dollar startup from the country without being limited to serving Southeast Asia or raising only from VCs in the region. Speaking of fundraising, you’d imagine that association has helped it win the continued support of GIC, which has been a key backer.
Now, Supabase has a real chance to put Singapore on the map for growing a global business in the age of AI.
India takes down Bitchat, Jack Dorsey’s app used by political protesters
Chat apps are a tough market to enter. There are hundreds of competitors and you need critical mass for a user to find value and return. Bitchat, the messaging app co-developed by Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey, has managed to beat the odds since its launch a year ago. Proof of that comes after it was removed from app stores in India .
Unlike other messaging apps, Bitchat uses Bluetooth to enable chat between devices meaning it can function without cellular signal or WiFi. That led to its popularity surging in India after it was used by protesters over the summer. Its features enabled the protesters, from a Gen Z-led group , to continue to communicate despite authorities cutting access to mobile networks in the area.

BY Venture Partners raises $60 million to back AI startups
My Startup World Staff
October 29, 2026
Comments Closed
0 like
BY Venture Partners, a global early-stage venture capital firm headquartered in Dubai, today announced the successful $60 million close of its third vehicle, Fund III. The fund is anchored by the Dubai Future District Fund (DFDF), with participation from established regional institutions, corporate venture arms, and prominent family offices, including leading regional player in AI and high-speed data infrastructure Multi Lane, Transmed Capital, and the Idriss Family Office (KSA). Fund III expands BY Venture Partners’s total Assets Under Management (AUM) to over $200 million.
Empowering AI-Native Founders from a Regional Powerhouse
Fund III will invest primarily up to $1m at the Pre-Seed to Series A stages into AI-native companies that reimagine enterprise workflows and scale globally from day one.
Headquartered in the UAE, BY Venture Partners operates from a region embracing AI at a pace. McKinsey’s November 2025 GCC survey found that 84% of organisations used AI in at least one business function, up from 62% in 2023. The firm invests across more than 16 international markets, with two-thirds of its capital deployed outside the MENA region across North America and Europe. Early momentum for Fund III is already underway, with 15 investments deployed to date out of a planned 40-company portfolio, including PQ Shield, Cosyne, Isometric, Huspy and Invisible.
“We are thrilled to officially announce Fund III today,” said Ghaith Yafi, Founding Partner at BY Venture Partners. “The focus of this fund is to back AI-native companies with global ambitions. We are particularly excited about the opportunity to attract some of the world’s most innovative AI companies into the Middle East and connect them with the region’s rapidly growing technology ecosystem. We are executing on a thesis designed to generate strong, long-term returns for our partners.”
Institutional backing for regional impact
The anchor commitment from DFDF reinforces BY Venture Partners’s role in elevating the Middle East as a global tech hub and bridging regional capital with international deal flow.
“We committed to Fund III because BY’s model works in both directions. It brings global AI-native companies into Dubai and takes founders from this region into international markets, and that exchange is what Dubai’s Economic Agenda D33 asks of us. Ghaith, Abdallah, Rami, Sohrab and the team have built and exited companies themselves and have managed capital through a full market cycle. The flow of companies and founders across that bridge is the basis on which we will measure this partnership,” said Nader Albastaki, Managing Director, Dubai Future District Fund (DFDF).
“We have been firm believers in BY Venture Partners since inception, and we are delighted to contribute to the firm’s Fund III, to help back up-and-coming AI-first startups in the region,” said MultiLane Founder and CEO Fadi Daou. “As an ecosystem builder myself, as well as a former entrepreneur, BY’s vision fully aligns with ours.”
Rebuilding Ecosystems: The Lebanese Angel Investor Network (LAIN)
Rooted in a commitment to ecosystem building, BY Venture Partners won the MITAI-backed mandate to manage and operate the Lebanese Angel Investor Network (LAIN). LAIN connects global diaspora capital with early-stage Lebanese founders, creating a structured pipeline for early-stage capital and connecting the next generation of regional angel investors. Demonstrating its long-term commitment to ecosystem recovery, BY will reinvest 50% of its carried interest directly back into rebuilding the Lebanese startup ecosystem.
Built by Founders, for Founders
BY sets itself apart through its operator-first DNA: all four partners – Ghaith Yafi, Abdallah Yafi, Rami Jisr and Sohrab Jahanbani – are repeat entrepreneurs who built and exited businesses before joining forces as investors. This hands-on, founder-centric approach has earned BY Venture Partners a Founder Net Promoter Score of 87.
BY’s track record has been built across more than one market cycle, including a full financial collapse in Lebanon, where Fund I carried significant exposure. That fund is still on course to return a strong multiple to its investors. The fund has had to adapt to fast-changing market conditions and has built a reputation for moving quickly to support founders in their most difficult and challenging days. Fund II continues to perform strongly relative to its vintage. Between them, the two funds have produced four unicorns, two from each, alongside a growing group of companies now valued in the hundreds of millions, and the firm has already returned meaningful capital to its LPs.
With Fund III, BY Venture Partners continues to leverage its global-first, AI-first network to give early-stage founders the operational edge, capital, and global connectivity required to build market-defining technology platforms.

What is fintech?
Fintech, or financial technology, is a term that describes the mobile applications , software and other technology that enable users and enterprises to access and manage their finances digitally.
It is also used interchangeably with the term fintech startup, which refers to a company whose core capability is in the development and/or delivery of fintech products and services.
As smartphones and other digital devices have gained popularity, fintech use cases have increased steadily. Today, popular mobile apps help people set financial goals, apply for mortgages, file taxes and much, much more. At the enterprise level, businesses across the financial industry are constantly on the lookout for ways to deploy fintech to increase their capabilities and offer more products and services to their customers.
The evolution of the term
The term "fintech", a combination of the words "finance" and "technology", was initially used by banks to describe technology that helped them track and manage their clients’ accounts. However, in the last five years, the term has shifted to include more consumer-related services, such as apps and software that are used to create budgets, track spending and buy and sell stocks.
Today, the term fintech can be used to describe technologies, services and companies in the financial sector that focus various capabilities, including retail banking, financial education, fundraising, cryptocurrencies, investment management and more.

candidates.text:
Tolan , the AI companion designed to help people manage their daily lives, navigate relationships and emotions, and accomplish their goals, has just expanded its runway with another $30 million in capital.
The startup’s investors in the latest round include Union Square Ventures, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew, doubling the total amount it has raised to date and pushing its valuation beyond the previous $120 million, according to a new report by Upstarts Media . (The startup didn’t disclose its new valuation, but PitchBook estimates it at more than $268 million, with “medium confidence.”)
Users engage with Tolan’s app through a cartoonish character that’s meant to offer support and help them get through their to-dos.
Image Credits: Tolan on App Store
Tolan generates revenue from its tiered memberships, which are required for full access to all features. The company told Upstarts Media its annual recurring revenue is now in the “double-digit millions.”
The startup is one of the few AI companions that have found some traction, as it claims to have more than 250,000 active users who have had more than 70 million conversations over the past year. Around 70% of its users are women, and 40% are parents, Tolan’s team told the news outlet. (Anecdotally, the app is said to appeal in particular to neurodivergent people , who may benefit from additional support, whether that’s emotional support or help with organizing tasks.)
Compared with other companions, Tolan seems to have found a balance between being helpful without being perceived as too weird. Compare that with the public shaming that Friend’s pendant-based AI companion faced; users dubbed Friend “ very cringe ,” The New York Times called it “hated,” and Wired said it “has no soul.”
Meanwhile, another former top contender in the space, Character.AI, recently filed for bankruptcy after its founder’s return to Google . (Its remaining staff is transitioning to Disney, which bought some of its assets.)
However, Tolan could end up facing increased competition from the more recent crop of AI agents, which help users plan, organize, and accomplish their tasks and goals, not just talk their way through them. For instance, Meta gave its AI agent Muse a cute avatar for its users to talk to, which it also plans to release as a hardware product in the future.
The startup also has to navigate the risks of offering AI-powered emotional support, given that multiple lawsuits have been filed against general-purpose AI app makers alleging that chatbot interactions contributed to users’ suicides.

candidates.title: Nirva Raises $25M Pre-Series A for an AI Pendant That Listens only to its Wearer
candidates.snippet: Nirva Raises $25M Pre-Series A for an AI Pendant That Listens only to its Wearer AI Funding Tracker
candidates.text:
Ambient AI is having a moment. Amazon launched a new wrist-worn device with Bee; a former Plaud exec launched ambient apps through a startup called Ambi, which aims to also build its own hardware; and Apple launched Voice Intelligence features during its iPhone launch in September. Now, a company called Nirva is betting on a jewelry-like pendant and its ability to listen only to the wearer.
The startup today announced a new $25 million pre-Series A round, adding to the $8 million it raised earlier in the year from investors like Lightspeed and South Park Commons, bringing its total raise to $33 million.
Nirva was founded in 2025 by two former Meta Reality Labs employees, Wei Lyu and Jason Chen, along with Hanying Hu, who founded a fashion and jewelry brand.
The company’s first device is a pendant, which can also be worn as a bracelet. The device weighs only around eight grams, making it easy to wear all day. Its battery lasts up to three days on a single charge.
Longer term, Nirva aims to release more devices.
Image Credits: Nirva
In a call with TechCrunch, Nirva CEO Lyu said that the company wanted to build a wearable that blends in with fashion, but also provides value to users.
“This is a piece of jewelry that only focuses on listening to your own speech. We are not like a voice recorder or like a meeting note taker. One key difference between us, Taya, Vocci, or Sandbar Ring is that we’re always passively listening to your own speech. So it’s always on. It keeps modeling the user and modeling your mind,” Lyu said.
For ambient devices, privacy is a big question, as people might not like to be recorded all the time. Plus, devices like the Ray-Ban Meta have instilled fear in those who are around the person wearing the smart glasses that they are being recorded too.
Nirva gets around this problem by asking users to record snippets of their voice during onboarding and building its model based on that. During use, the device filters out conversations or data captured from the other people around the device. That means it’s only recording the wearer.
In addition, Nirva by default doesn’t keep any audio data or transcripts after processing the conversations.
Nirva is positioning itself as a personal insights company rather than a productivity startup. However, its app shows you reminders or action items and ways to act on them. Lyu said that through its app, the startup wants to help users show up for others in a better way in their lives.
“I think there’s no universal way to help everyone to solve their problems. We are building a tool to help people to improve their self-understanding, self-compassion, and self-awareness,” Lyu said.
Image Credits: Nirva
The companion app parses users’ speech and creates insights that it infers are related to the user’s personality, including patterns, the people who tend to be around them, the places they’ve been to, and other daily notes. Lyu emphasized that the app shows users insights around their emotions, communication style, and ways they can improve.
Lyu gave an example of an incident when she forgot to thank her mother for something, and the app later nudged her with a reminder about this.
The company also said that, before it discards the audio, it’s able to track the tone, pitch, volume, and speed, which are useful for deriving emotion-related understandings that are then surfaced in the app.
Nirva will start taking orders for its devices in November, with an aim to ship them to early users by the end of the year. The $249 device will be available in silver, brushed silver, black, and gold.
The startup has competition in the AI wearables area. There are companies like former Apple employees’ Taya , which is also building intelligent jewelry. Plus, startups like Friend and Bee are trying to be companion gadgets as well.

Whedon served as an executive producer , along with Tim Minear . The series is set in the year 2517, after the arrival of humans in a new star system, [ 1 ] and follows the adventures of the renegade crew of Serenity , a " Firefly -class" spaceship . The ensemble cast portrays the nine characters living aboard Serenity . Whedon pitched the show as "nine people looking into the blackness of space and seeing nine different things." [ 2 ] The show explores the lives of a group of people, some of whom fought on the losing side of a civil war , making a living on the fringes of society as part of their star system's pioneer culture. The two surviving superpowers, the United States and China, united to form the central federal government, called the Alliance . According to Whedon's vision, "Nothing will change in the future: Technology will advance, but we will still have the same political, moral, and ethical problems as today." [ 3 ] Firefly premiered in the United States on the Fox network on September 20, 2002. By mid-December, it had averaged 4.7 million viewers per episode and was 98th in Nielsen ratings . [ 4 ] It was canceled after 11 of the 14 produced episodes were aired. Despite its short run, it received strong sales when it was released on DVD and has large fan support campaigns. [ 5 ] [ 6 ] It won a Primetime Emmy Award in 2003 for Outstanding Special Visual Effects for a Series . TV Guide ranked it No. 5 on their 2013 list of 60 "shows that were canceled too soon". [ 7 ] [ 8 ] The show's post-airing success led Whedon and Universal Pictures to produce Serenity , a 2005 film that continues the story from the series. [ 5 ] The Firefly franchise expanded into other media, including comics and two tabletop role-playing games . [ 9 ] [ 10 ] On March 15, 2026, star Nathan Fillion confirmed that an animated series was in development with animation by ShadowMachine . Premise [ edit ] Backstory [ edit ] The series takes place in the year 2517, on a variety of planets with numerous habitable moons. The TV series does not reveal whether these celestial bodies are within one star system, only saying that Serenity ' s mode of propulsion through space is a "gravity-drive". Each episode begins with either Book or Captain Reynolds providing the backstory. Book's narration runs as follows: [ 11 ] After the Earth was used up, we found a new solar system, and hundreds of new Earths were terraformed and colonized. The central planets formed the Alliance and decided all the planets had to join under their rule. There was some disagreement on that point. After the war, many of the Independents who had fought and lost drifted to the edges of the system, far from Alliance control. Out here, people struggle to get by with the most basic technologies. A ship would bring you work. A gun would help you keep it. A captain's goal was simple: Find a crew. Find a job. Keep flying. —   Derrial Book, introductory narrative for the show The film Serenity reveals that the planets and moons are in an extensive system, and production documents related to the film indicate that there is no faster-than-light travel in this universe . The characters occasionally refer to "Earth-that-was" and the film establishes that, long before the events in the series, a large population had emigrated from Earth to a new star system in generation ships : [ 12 ] "Earth-that-was could no longer sustain our numbers, we were so many." The emigrants established themselves in this new star system, with "dozens of planets and hundreds of moons", and many of these were terraformed , a process that was only the first step in making a planet habitable. The outlying settlements often did not receive support in the construction of their civilizations. This resulted in many border planets and moons having forbidding, dry environments, well-suited to the Western genre.
